title: Super versus Savings accounts
body:
O.P.
I'm 61. Maxed on Super concessions available including the 3-year bring forward. I have 1m in Super, 600k in shares (VGS, VAS and VDHG). And 600k in 3 different savings accounts, all bringing in 5% interest. I haven't yet contributed the $32,500 into Super for this year but plan on taking it from one of the savings accounts. Up until now I was a bit nervous about adding it to super in case it all dropped with the ME war but feel a bit more confident now (fingers crossed). My question is (and perhaps this is hard for any of us to answer!) do I take more from savings to put into my ETFs? The ETFs are relatively new to me (last year) so I'm feeling my way with them, but reasonably happy that they have stayed on an upward trend.

Up until now I was a bit nervous about adding it to super in case it all dropped with the ME war
Money in Super doesn't mean it's all in shares. Even if you were 100% certain that the stockmarket was going to fall, have a look at the investment options your Super provider offers and you'll see that they have choices that insulate you from that.
do I take more from savings to put into my ETFs?
Like above, you can choose to invest those savings into the same kind of assets within Super instead of outside to get the same kind returns but with a massive tax benefit instead, especially in light of the recent budget changes. The downside is obviously having that money locked away until preservation age, but in your case that's a mere 0-4 years away.

[User #8130713008 postsandrew99999PassiveInvestingAustralia.comWhirlpool Forums Addict] abcd123 writes...
I'm feeling my way with them
It is easy to get confused since there are two separate dimensions you're talking about (without realising)
The investment selection – can be Aussie stocks (e.g. VAS), International stocks (e.g. VGS), Property, Bonds, Cash, a fund with a combination of any or all of those
The structure/investment vehicle that can hold investments – can be held in super, in your own name, in a trust, or in a company.
So, you can hold the same investments in your own name as you can in super.
So you need to answer two separate questions
Which structure – hold it in super or own name
Access – super is inaccessible until you meet a condition of release, including being retired and over 60, ceasing any employment arrangement while over 60, or being over 65 regardless. The exception is for those over 60, you can still withdraw up to 10% p.a. if you need it, even if you don't meet the other conditions of release.
Tax – if you can make concessional contributions (cap is 32.5k p.a. inc. employer contributions) and your taxable income is over $45k pa, then you can get massive returns by way of paying less tax
What to invest in (shares, stocks, etc.)
Growth assets – typically provide higher returns but with higher volatility
Defensive assets – provide more stability (lower volatility) but with lower long-term returns
You should find a proportion of each that you can hold even through periods of global turmoil because chopping and changing ends up far worse than finding a good portfolio that suits the level of risk you can tolerate and sticking to it no matter what happens in the world.
[User #18356030340 postspgdownloadWhirlpool Forums Addict] abcd123 writes...
Up until now I was a bit nervous about adding it to super in case it all dropped
Shares (and super) go up and down. For the beginner the trick is to focus on diversifying (you already are – super and index funds are highly diversified). Also not to try time the market or sell everything when there's a correction (thus cementing any loses)
You are extremely well place for a very comfortable retirement. The main reason to put money into super now (as always) is to minimise tax on your wealth. That's why there are limits on how much you can put in otherwise rich people would just put all their money in it.
Right now you don't really have to do anything more and there's definitely no need to do anything risky to get a last minute retirement return. Just keep the simple rule in that mind risk increases as the (possible) return increases. Banks pay 5% and are 100% safe. Index funds and super pay 8% and a also pretty reliable. Anything above 10% is getting adventurous.
Also don't confuse volatility with risk. Shares etc. go up and down all the time, some less so than others. Solid shares (and super) tend to drift up on average over time.
Perhaps get some professional advise. There's lots of tricks and traps as you transition to retirement. Just don't take specific investment advise (i.e. you should buy share X and company Y) and you should get a better understanding. Also go read this: Retirement Made Simple
But otherwise you're doing fine. Just keep topping up your current investment vehicles (esp. super) and also put aside $100K or so into a HISA earning 5% that you can use for a year if the markets go south for a while.
